To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) student ratings of instructor effectiveness correlate positively with student motivation to learn, student satisfaction with course, student learning of subject-matter content, and student learning of problem-solving skills; (2) these four outcome measures account for 40 percent to 50 percent of the variance in mean student ratings; and (3) these four outcome variables, in combination, account for only 10 percent to 15 percent of the variance shared with a composite of objective measures of student performance.

(a) the amount of unaccounted variance in mean student ratings after discounting shared variance with objective measures of learning is about 80 percent, and (b) this variance can be reduced by 50 percent or more if we use a set of outcome measures that includes motivation as well as learning.

(1) the variance in student ratings that is unaccounted for by measures of student learning and motivation is not due to measurement error; and (2), the variance in student overall effectiveness ratings that is unexplained by measures of student outcomes is not due to random error.
